meta.note: All figures provisional and subject to revision by the issuing statistical office.

markets.name: United Kingdom
markets.commentary: Headline cooled to 2.6% from 2.8%, the lowest since March 2025, on softer transport and motor fuel costs; core held flat at 2.6%. Factory gate (output) prices eased to 3.5% from a revised 3.7%, still ahead of CPI but the gap is narrowing. The input side confirms last month's energy call: crude oil inputs slowed to 42.3% year on year from a revised 82.1%, and fell 20.8% in the month, the steepest monthly drop since April 2020. Services producer prices, by contrast, firmed to 4.3% for Q2, so cost pressure is migrating from energy into labour-heavy services.

markets.name: Euro Area
markets.commentary: Inflation fell to 2.8% from 3.2%, ending three straight monthly rises; core (ex energy, food, alcohol and tobacco) eased to 2.4% from 2.6%. Energy's contribution dropped to 8.5% year on year from 10.8%, confirming last month's call that the May energy spike had peaked. Services stayed firm at 3.2%. Producer prices (May, latest published) at 5.9% year on year still run well above the June CPI print, so some pipeline pressure has not yet cleared the system. June euro area PPI is due early August.

markets.name: United States
markets.commentary: The sharp reversal of last month's alarm. Headline fell 0.4% on the month, the largest single-month drop since April 2020, taking the annual rate down to 3.5% from 4.2%. Core was flat on the month and steady at 2.6% year on year, so the swing is almost entirely energy: PPI final demand energy dropped 6.4% in the month, with gasoline down about 12% and accounting for roughly two-thirds of the fall. PPI final demand itself fell 0.3% on the month but is still up 5.5% year on year. The pass-through risk flagged last month has not materialised, at least not yet, but the size of the swing shows how energy-dependent both prints remain.

markets.name: Japan
markets.commentary: Moving the wrong way for a second month. Headline rose to 1.7% from 1.5%; the core-core measure (ex fresh food and energy) eased only slightly to 1.7% from 1.8%, while the narrower ex-fresh-food-only core ticked up to 1.6% from 1.4%. CGPI accelerated again to 7.1% year on year from 6.3%, up 0.4% on the month, led by petroleum and coal products, electric power and gas, and plastics, with the import price index up 29.7% year on year on a yen basis as the weak yen keeps landing costs high. Government subsidies are still holding the shelf number down; the factory gate keeps running hotter, not cooler.

euroMembers.name: Germany
euroMembers.note: Eased sharply to 2.4% from 2.7% as energy cooled further, core down slightly to 2.5%. Producer prices near-level with consumer prices at 2.2%, the gap that was already narrow last month has now nearly closed.

euroMembers.name: France
euroMembers.note: Dropped sharply to 2.0% from 2.8% as energy fell to 11.0% year on year from 16.6%. Core eased further too, to 1.0% from 1.6%, so the disinflation here is broad, not just energy.

euroMembers.name: Italy
euroMembers.note: Eased slightly to 3.0% from 3.2%, core down to 1.6%. Still the odd one out on energy: non-regulated energy accelerated to 13.3% from 12.5% and regulated energy jumped to 9.2% from 5.6%. Producer prices remain the hottest of the four at 7.3%, up from 6.8%.

euroMembers.name: Spain
euroMembers.note: Stuck at 3.6% for a third straight month, the only one of the four not benefiting from the energy pullback. Housing (electricity and gas) is the main driver; core down only a touch, to 2.9% from 3.0%.

euroMembersNote: Headline HICP year on year is shown on the comparable Eurostat basis (final June 2026 release, published 17 July). Core measures differ slightly by national office (broadly excluding energy and food). PPI is held at May 2026 for all four to stay comparable with the euro area aggregate (+5.9%), which is the latest published month; the June euro area figure is due early August. On that May basis: Germany +2.2%, Italy +7.3%. France and Spain country PPI are not in the headline release and are marked n/a.

signals.title: The US reversed hard on energy; Japan is moving the other way
signals.observe: US headline CPI fell from 4.2% to 3.5% year on year with a -0.4% monthly print, the sharpest since April 2020, driven by a 6.4% monthly drop in PPI energy and gasoline down about 12%. In the same month, Japan's CGPI accelerated from 6.3% to 7.1% while its CPI actually ticked up, from 1.5% to 1.7%.
signals.why: Last month's call that Brent had peaked and was rolling over has now shown up cleanly in the US numbers. It has not reached Japan yet, where a weak yen and import costs (up 29.7% year on year, yen basis) are still pushing producer prices higher even as subsidies hold the shelf price down.
signals.action: Treat the May US spike as transitory when reviewing any pricing or surcharge clauses tied to it. Keep stress-testing Japan-linked input costs against the 7.1% CGPI figure, not the 1.7% CPI headline; that gap is still widening, not closing.

signals.title: Europe's disinflation is broad, but Spain isn't sharing in it
signals.observe: Euro area headline fell to 2.8% from 3.2%. Germany down to 2.4% (from 2.7%), France down to 2.0% (from 2.8%), Italy down to 3.0% (from 3.2%). Spain alone held flat at 3.6%, with the highest core of the four at 2.9%.
signals.why: Everywhere else the fall is being driven by energy rolling over. Spain's pressure is coming from housing, mainly electricity and gas, which is a stickier, less energy-spot-price-driven component.
signals.action: Don't read the euro area aggregate as representative of Spain specifically. Anything Spain-weighted (pricing, wage indexation, contract escalators) should be modelled off Spain's own 3.6%/2.9% figures, not the bloc average.

signals.title: Producer-consumer gaps are closing in Europe, still wide open in Japan and the US
signals.observe: Germany's PPI (May, 2.2%) and HICP (June, 2.4%) are now nearly level, down from a much wider gap in recent months. UK PPI (3.5%) vs CPI (2.6%) has also narrowed noticeably from May. Japan's CGPI (7.1%) vs CPI (1.7%) and US PPI (5.5%) vs CPI (3.5%) remain wide.
signals.why: In Europe, the pipeline pressure flagged last month has largely fed through or eased alongside falling energy costs. In Japan and the US it hasn't, so more cost is still sitting with suppliers, either as a margin hit or a bill still to be passed on.
signals.action: European supplier renegotiations can likely step back to a normal cadence. Keep the urgency on Japan- and US-linked contracts flagged last month; those gaps haven't closed.

US CPI and PPI for July 2026: mid August 2026
